transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-14
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Ethan (LumenPay Lead Eng), Sandra (CTO), Raj (DevOps), Maya G. (Prod)

Summary:
Quick orientation to Redwood hosted chat API focused on streaming behavior, parameterization for latency/cost tradeoffs, and retry/failover patterns. SE demoed live streaming session from the sandbox, showed console trace for token-level timing, and walked through retry/backoff and fallback to cheaper model variants. Customer asked about SSO, data retention, and private deployment options; team committed to baseline tests and sharing security docs.

Topics:
- Hosted chat streaming behavior, partial tokens, and client-side handling
- Parameters to control latency vs. completeness (max_tokens, stop, temperature, top_p)
- Retry strategies, idempotency, and resume/handshake patterns
- Console traces, token-level cost breakdowns, and Optimize suggestions
- Security: SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS encryption at rest/in transit

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you taking the time. I see Sandra and Ethan are on—hi. I'm maya with Redwood, AE, and Diego from SE will run through a short demo then we'll leave time for questions.
[00:18] Sandra (CTO): Yep thanks, hi. We've got about 45 minutes, Raj needs to step out around 15:30 but he'll stay for the parts about retries and k8s autoscale.
[00:34] Diego (SE): Cool, I'll share my screen. Quick agenda: 1) live streaming call 2) parameters and tuning 3) retry/playbook and fallbacks 4) console + Optimize highlights.
[00:52] Ethan (Lead Eng): For context we run payments chatflows and want sub-300ms p95 on short confirmations, but can tolerate 1s for longer flows. Also curious how token caching works for repeated prompts.
[01:12] Maya (AE): Perfect, and can you confirm expected qps? 
[01:18] Ethan: Burst to 150 qps, baseline 30 qps, peak day-to-day.
[01:25] Diego: Good, thanks. I'll do a quick generation to show streaming. I'm calling the hosted chat endpoint with stream=true, messages includes context and we set max_tokens low to keep latency.
[01:48] Diego: (typing) You'll see chunked events — sometimes called delta events — arriving as the model decodes. Note that depending on model variant we buffer small segments; this is controllable with 'streaming_chunk_size' and 'nucleus' but names in your SDK map to stream options.
[02:12] Ethan: Quick question — if the stream cuts off, what's the recommended client behavior? Reconnect?
[02:20] Diego: Good question. Best practice: treat the call as resumable if you have idempotency keys and the server-side kv cache can resume from last token. Otherwise client should request fallback with reply partial response + delta. We also surface a resume token in the event metadata — although, small caveat, in some transcripts that field is transcribed as 'resume token' but SDK surface may call it 'cursor' or 'offset', so you'll see different names across libs.
[02:50] Raj (DevOps): K-V cash? Sorry, K-V cash — do you mean KV cache?
[02:56] Diego: Yes, yes, KV cache. Sometimes the transcriber writes 'K-V cash' haha. The KV cache stores previous key-values to speed up context for long conversations and avoid re-encoding.
[03:14] Diego: I'll trigger a longer completion that yields streaming across multiple events — watch timing in the console.
[03:45] (screen shows tokens streaming; console trace visible)
[04:02] Diego: See here: token timing column, per-token latency, and aggregate token cost. For your short confirmations, you can tune prompt templates and set max_output_tokens to 16-32 which keeps p95 down.
[04:28] Ethan: And batching? We're worried about tradeoffs if we batch requests for cost savings but spike latency.
[04:36] Diego: Right — Redwood supports continuous batching at the runtime layer; the console shows when a request was batched. There're autoscaling knobs to prioritize latency (dedicated lanes) or cost (batch more aggressively). For hosted usage you can pick a policy: latency-first vs cost-first.
[05:05] Sandra: If we pick cost-first and a user waits too long, do we get fallback to a cheaper model?
[05:12] Maya (AE): Yes — we can set routing policies to fallback to a cheaper quantized variant when latency SLOs can still be met, or fallback to a higher-latency but lower-cost path. Diego will demo automatic fallback later.
[05:35] Diego: Next I'll intentionally throttle the stream to show reconnect and retry behavior. In this test I'll simulate a transient 503.
[05:52] (short pause, click)
[06:04] Diego: Simulated 503 — the SDK will attempt exponential backoff by default. For streaming, the client should re-open with the same idempotency key and request resume; if resume is unavailable server will indicate last stable token index and we can replay suffix.
[06:36] Raj: For Kubernetes, if a node restarts mid-stream, does Redwood re-route behind the scenes?
[06:44] Diego: For the hosted plane yes — we automatically route to healthy backends and if necessary fallback to model variants. In private deployments the control plane offers similar behavior but needs the private router configured.
[07:05] Ethan: Can you show the console view for retries?
[07:11] Diego: Sure — here's the trace: you can see initial attempt, then a retry record with reason '502 gateway' and an automatic fallback to model 'rwd-lite-1q' for the second attempt. Also shows cost delta between attempts.
[07:33] Sandra: On the security side, what about logs? We need auditability.
[07:39] Maya: We provide request-level metadata, token-level billing, and audit logs. For enterprise tiers we retain extended logs and integrate with customer SIEM via syslog or S3 export. Also we have SOC2 Type II; Diego can attach the security pack.
[08:00] Diego: I'll drop a link in the chat to SOC2, encryption, and SSO docs after the call.
[08:10] Ethan: Do you support SAML/SSO for console and role-based access?
[08:15] Maya: Yes, SAML SSO + SCIM provisioning and fine-grained RBAC. We also support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for private deployments.
[08:29] Raj: For data residency we may need EU-only. How does hosted handle region pinning?
[08:36] Diego: We support region routing — requests can be pinned to eu-west or us-east; policy routing will keep data in-region for storage and logs. For stricter needs we recommend Redwood Private.
[08:52] (Diego shares sandbox credentials)
[09:05] Diego: Now I'm going to adjust streaming_chunk_size and show how smaller chunks reduce perceived latency but increase overhead/cost.
[09:22] Diego: Here, chunk size 1 = more frequent deltas; chunk size 4 = less frequent but larger payloads. For rapid confirmations we recommend tiny chunk sizes with low max_tokens.
[09:40] Ethan: Any best practice for stop sequences in transactional messages? We have disclaimers and trailing prompts.
[09:46] Diego: Use explicit stop tokens and consider 'echo' behavior to avoid repeating prompt text; also check model-specific quirks — some models honor stop earlier than others. The console Optimize tab can suggest stop tokens after analyzing sample prompt/response pairs.
[10:12] Sandra: What's the edge case if stream starts but never finishes?
[10:18] Diego: If there's no finalization event, we treat it as partial. Clients must implement a timeout; on server side we will eventually mark the generation as aborted and surface the partial response. You'll get an error code and can trigger a retry with same idempotency key.
[10:44] Ethan: About idempotency keys — what's the best shape? UUID per user-turn?
[10:50] Diego: UUID per intent-turn is ideal. Include a small logical nonce and timestamp; the server keeps keys for a short retention window (configurable).
[11:05] (screen: Console -> Optimize)
[11:12] Diego: Optimize will analyze your usage and suggest quantization and batching settings. For LumenPay's workload it might recommend 4-bit quantized variant for non-sensitive background tasks.
[11:32] Sandra: Is quality impacted?
[11:34] Diego: Slightly, we measure quality deltas and you can run evals within the console to see regression thresholds. Redwood can flag quality regressions before deployment.
[11:50] Ethan: Can we do canary rollouts?
[11:55] Maya: Yes, rollouts are supported: canary, A/B, and automatic rollback on metrics. Console exposes per-model rollout controls and health checks.
[12:10] Raj: For the pilot, we'll want a dedicated slot during business hours to ensure latency -- can you reserve?
[12:18] Maya: For pilots, we can reserve a small dedicated pool or priority lanes in hosted. We'll confirm pricing.
[12:28] Diego: Back to retries — here's a quick diagram: client retry -> server checks idempotency -> if cache present resume, else fallback to new generation. If fallback model differs, we note it in trace and you can compare outputs.
[12:50] Ethan: How do you handle token accounting when resuming? Do we double-bill?
[12:56] Diego: Billing is per generated token; if a retry replays tokens only once billing will reflect final net generated tokens. We try to avoid double-billing by attributing replay tokens to server-side deduplication when resume succeeds.
[13:17] Sandra: What about streaming over websockets vs chunked HTTP? We use websockets in product.
[13:24] Diego: Both supported. Websockets keep a persistent connection which is great for low-latency streaming and reduces handshake overhead; chunked HTTP/2 SSE works well for serverless clients. Resume semantics are available for both but the mechanism differs: resume token vs reconnect id.
[13:48] Ethan: Can you show a small code snippet of a client reconnect?
[13:54] Diego: (reads) pseudocode: open stream with idempotency_key; on error, backoff; re-open with same key and resume=true; if resume false -> start new request. The SDKs wrap this pattern so most teams don't implement manual resume.
[14:20] (Diego posts a link to SDK retry docs)
[14:30] Maya: Quick check — are there specific compliance docs you need beyond SOC2?
[14:36] Sandra: We need HIPAA consideration for certain endpoints, and an NDA before sending real sample data.
[14:42] Maya: Understood; we'll route that to legal. For HIPAA we recommend Redwood Private or strict hosted contract terms.
[14:55] Ethan: For sandbox testing, what's the typical latency difference vs production?
[15:02] Diego: Sandbox is shared and may be slower; plan for +20-40ms p95 overhead. Production dedicated lanes will be lower and predictable.
[15:18] Raj: About autoscale: will pods spin up fast enough for a sudden 150 qps burst?
[15:24] Diego: With reserved capacity yes; autoscale on shared hosting has a small ramp—if you need immediate headroom choose a burst plan or dedicated pool.
[15:38] (Diego switches to a demo showing an intentional 502 then automatic fallback)
[16:00] Diego: See here: a 502 triggers immediate retry and fallback to lighter quantized model; user sees minimal delay. The console flags user impact and shows affected routes.
[16:26] Maya G. (Product): From product POV, how do we reconcile occasional quality drift when falling back? We need detection when answers degrade.
[16:34] Diego: Console has quality monitoring tied to prompt sets and evals. You can create regression alerts and tie them to rollbacks.
[16:49] Sandra: For the pilot, we'll want a stability SLO and a rollback threshold.
[16:56] Maya (AE): We can help configure SLOs in the console and run an initial 72-hour pilot to gather metrics.
[17:06] Ethan: What's the ramp for private deployments? We may choose that later.
[17:11] Diego: Private deployments take longer — typically 6-8 weeks for on-prem with KMS and networking. VPC-based private can be shorter 3-4 weeks.
[17:25] Raj: Any known gotchas with KMS integration and Kubernetes?
[17:30] Diego: Make sure KMS permissions are scoped for the node role and that rotation is coordinated; we'll provide a checklist.
[17:44] (short silence; Diego runs an optimize suggestion demo)
[18:05] Diego: Optimize suggests increasing batching for background scoring jobs and lowering chunk size for interactive flows; it also predicts cost impact.
[18:20] Ethan: Could you estimate cost delta if we go from hosted to a small dedicated pool?
[18:28] Maya: We'll put a custom estimate in the follow-up pricing sheet. Quick rule: dedicated reduces per-token cost at scale but has a commit. For pilot size you may see 10-25% savings depending on utilization.
[18:46] Sandra: Any vendor lock concerns? We like portability.
[18:51] Maya: Redwood exports model bundles and the runtime config; and with Private you run same runtime. We avoid lock-in by making model artifacts portable and providing migration docs.
[19:10] Ethan: I'd like Diego to run our sample payloads through a baseline; we can share a subset of logs.
[19:16] Diego: Great — please share sanitized payloads or sample templates. We'll run them and report p50/p95 and token counts.
[19:28] Raj: Could we get a short live run now with a small batch of 10?
[19:32] Diego: Sure, kicking off 10 requests. (typing) Outputs streaming — latency results populating.
[20:02] Diego: Results: median 120ms, p95 340ms for these short prompts in the sandbox. As noted sandbox overhead applies.
[20:18] Ethan: Those look promising; pilot target is p95 < 300ms in production.
[20:23] Diego: With dedicated lanes we can meet that, given proper prompt truncation and chunking.
[20:35] Sandra: About retention — logs and prompts — can you auto-redact?
[20:41] Maya: We offer field-level redact and PII detection pipelines; you can configure auto-redact rules in the ingestion layer.
[20:55] Ethan: Are embeddings in scope for us? We'll use for reranking some receipts.
[21:01] Diego: Yes, Redwood embeddings are supported; Optimize can recommend dimensionality vs cost tradeoff.
[21:14] (Diego shows a console alert for a simulated rollout)
[21:26] Diego: Example: during a canary a quality regression was caught and rollback occurred automatically. The console shows diff and responsible commit.
[21:44] Ethan: Great. Any docs on SDK retry knobs?
[21:48] Diego: I'll put the SDK retry doc link in the chat. (link posted)
[21:56] Raj: For SLA, if we see repeated falls to fallback model, do we get credits?
[22:02] Maya: SLAs for dedicated include uptime and latency guarantees; credits apply per contract terms. We'll include SLA wording in the pilot contract.
[22:18] Sandra: Ok next steps?
[22:22] Maya: Recap: 1) Diego runs baseline with your sample payloads; 2) Maya sends security pack and pricing; 3) schedule a 1-hour pilot kickoff next week.
[22:34] Ethan: Sounds good.
[22:38] Maya G.: We'll prepare a short success criteria doc for pilot.
[22:44] Diego: One final tip — instrument at the request level and capture token-level times for better diagnostics; console integrates with open tracing.
[22:58] (meeting moves into questions and quick clarifications, small crosstalk)
[30:00] Sandra: Quick Q — is there a way to simulate degraded network for our app?
[30:08] Diego: Yes, we can replay throttled traces in the sandbox. We'll include a script.
[31:20] (lots of minor back-and-forth, clarifications, some overlapping speech)
[40:12] Ethan: Thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[40:18] Maya: Thank you — we'll follow up with materials and the sandbox invite.
[40:25] (meeting wraps; final notes about legal and HIPAA follow-up)
